analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to test drinking-water contaminants for hormone-disrupting effects and post results publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote: it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the EPA to expand its screening program for endocrine disruptors—chemicals that interfere with hormones—to any substance that may be in sources of drinking water. It set deadlines for a testing plan, prioritized substances posing the greatest public health risk, required a public searchable database of results, let citizens petition to have a chemical fast-tracked for testing, and authorized $5 million a year for five years to do the work. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and then to a subcommittee a week later, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks water from public systems, especially groups more vulnerable to hormone-disrupting chemicals: infants, children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with serious illness histories. The bill directed EPA to prioritize exactly those groups when deciding what to test first, and its public database would have let ordinary people and local officials see what was being found and what EPA did about it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required EPA, within one year, to publish a plan and schedule for testing all substances on the Drinking Water Preliminary Contaminant Candidate List and all substances with a national drinking water regulation, prioritizing those posing the greatest public health concern to groups like infants, children, and pregnant women [S2][S3].

It would have extended mandatory testing to any substance that may be found in drinking water sources and to which a substantial population may be exposed, closing a gap where the existing program under the food and pesticide law did not cover drinking-water contaminants [S2][S3].

It would have required EPA to publish a publicly searchable database within 180 days showing which substances were selected for testing, test orders, deadlines, and results, and to decide within six months of receiving test results whether to take regulatory action [S2][S3].

It would have given any person the right to petition EPA to add a substance to the testing plan or force accelerated testing of a chemical suspected of being an endocrine disruptor found in drinking water, with EPA required to grant or deny the petition within 90 days [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, pesticide registrants, and importers whose substances fell under the expanded testing program would have paid the cost of testing, though the bill let companies form consortia to share those costs through binding arbitration [S3]. The federal government would have appropriated up to $5 million per year for fiscal years 2012 through 2016 to run the program [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill allowed companies required to test to rely on data 'prepared or provided by any person' in place of new testing, including data from the manufacturers themselves, which could have slowed or complicated EPA's evaluations even as it avoided duplicative testing [S3].

It carried real compliance costs for chemical manufacturers and importers, which supporters of industry would argue raise production costs, and set a 10-year schedule for testing all covered substances—long enough that some harmful exposures could continue for a decade before results were in [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health case was straightforward: hormone-disrupting chemicals in drinking water are linked to reproductive and developmental harm, and the existing screening program did not systematically cover drinking-water contaminants. The costs fell mainly on the industries that make the chemicals, with $5 million a year of public money—small by federal standards. The main design weakness was that industry-supplied data could substitute for independent testing, and the 10-year timeline was slow relative to the risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy a week later, and it never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Markey introduced the bill on February 8, 2011, with Representatives Grijalva, Moran, and Norton as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S3][S5].
On February 15, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy; no further action was ever recorded for the remainder of the 112th Congress [S5].
The bill's cosponsor list never grew beyond eight members, all Democrats, and no companion action is recorded in the Senate [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical and pesticide manufacturers who would have faced mandatory testing of drinking-water-related substances are better off, since no test orders or public database were ever required. Ordinary water drinkers gained nothing, because the screening gap the bill targeted remained open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers; the screening gap stayed open

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but all eight cosponsors were Democrats and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican, so the pattern, to the extent the record shows one, split by party.

industries.note: The bill would have required testing of any substance that may be in drinking water sources and exposed to a substantial population, with manufacturers and importers bearing the testing costs. Its outcome left them free of new test orders and left the public without the results database.

The endocrine screening program the bill expanded runs under the food and pesticide law, so pesticide makers would have faced additional test orders and cost-sharing obligations. The bill died, so those costs were never imposed.
A 10-year national testing schedule would have generated a steady stream of contracted toxicology work. The program was never funded, so the work never materialized.
